caseno: Writ Petition No. 2948 of 1992 with Writ Petition No. 1876 of 1992.
lawyer:
MA Wahab Miah, Advocate — For the Petitioner in WP No. 2948 of 1992. 
M I Furuqui, Advocate — For the Petitioner in WP No. 1876 of 1992. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan Additional Attorney-General, with Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General — For the Respondents
parties:
Akhtari Begum and another ------  Petitioners
vs.
Court of Settlement and another ------  Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J : These two Rules issued in Writ Petition No. 2948 of 1992 and Writ Petition No. 1870 of 1992 were heard together and are being disposed of by one judgment in view of the fact that both the writ petitions have arisen out of the same judgment of the Court of Settlement, Dhaka.

2. Both the Rules were issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 25-4-92 passed by the Respondent No. 1, the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka, in Case No. 190 of 1987 and Case No. 1026 of 1988 in respect of House No. 51, Bonogram Road, Sutrapur, Dhaka, should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

3. In Writ Petition No. 2948 of 1992 one Akhtari Begum and her son Md. Iqbal are the petitioners. It is the case of the petitioners that they are citizens of Bangladesh and they are residing at House No. 21/3, Avenue-3, Block-A, Section-11, Mirpur, Dhaka. The property in question is situated at House No. 51, Bonogram Road, PS Sutrapur, Dhaka, comprising an area of 0.34 decimals of land with the building standing thereon. The property in question was acquired by Md. Ishaque, the husband of the petitioner No. 1 Akhtari Begum and father of the petitioner No. 2 Md. Iqbal. Md. Ishaque acquired the property by a registered deed of perpetual lease being No. 4648 dated 7-4-1958 and also by purchase of the rent receiving interest (suit rent) by a registered deed of sale being No. 4649 dated 7-4-1958 from Sree Sree Gouranga Dev Bigraha (Deity) represented by its Shebait who got the same by a registered sale deed dated 13-2-1943 from Sreemati Hemangini Devi. After purchasing the same late Md. Ishaque was residing there with his family members. Petitioner No. 2 Md. Iqbal was born in the same property on 16-12-1962. Md. Ishaque died on 24-8-1967 leaving the present petitioners as only heirs. After the death of Md. Ishaque the petitioners had been in possession of the property in question till 16th December, 1971 when they were ousted by their tenants and miscreants and since then were out of possession of the property.

4. When the law and order situation became a bit normal, the petitioner No. 1 applied to the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South) Dhaka, praying for giving back the possession of the property in question. But, ultimately, no action was taken on the application filed by the petitioner No. 1. Thereafter in 1975 the petitioner No. 1 came to know that the tenants who were in possession in the suit property got the property declared as abandoned property and thereafter they took allotment from the Government. Then the petitioner No. 1 applied to the Secretary, Ministry of Works on 4-11-1975 praying for releasing the property from the list of abandoned property. The Ministry by its letter dated 15-11-1975 asked the petitioner to submit the papers before the Ministry within seven days from the date of receipt of the said letter. Unfortunately, the said letter was addressed at 51, Bonogram Road, Sutrapur, Dhaka and as such, the tenants who were hostile to the petitioners suppressed the said letter, in collusion with the peon and subsequently the petitioners could not have filed the papers as desired by the Ministry. Again, the petitioner filed an application on 19-9-1976 to the Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Works praying for releasing the property from the list of abandoned property. But no step was taken by the Ministry upon the aforesaid application.

5. In the meantime, the Ordinance 54 of 1985 was promulgated making the provisions for publishing the list of abandoned properties and accordingly, the property in question was enlisted in ''ka'' list published on 23rd September, 1986. Before the Court of Settlement the petitioners filed application for releasing the property and that case was numbered as Case No. 190 of 1987. The petitioners also sold a portion of the land by an agreement in the year 1970 to one Mesbahuddin Ahmed, that is, ''0501 Ajutangsha. Since the petitioner failed to execute and register the sale deed, aforesaid Mesbahuddin Ahmed filed a suit for specific performance of contract, namely, Title Suit No. 160 of 1972 and got the kabala registered through Court vide Execution Case No. 9 of 1975 in respect of the portion of the land which the petitioners agreed to sell to him. This Mesbahuddin is the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 1876 of 1992.

6. Government contested the case without filing any written statement contending that the petitioners left this country and started living in Pakistan and, as such, they are Pakistani citizens, the property was legally taken over as abandoned property. The petitioners examined two witnesses including petitioner No. 1 herself and the Government also examined two witnesses in their favour. In support of the claim of the petitioners they have filed all the relevant papers and documents to the Court of Settlement. After hearing the matter and perusing the materials the Court of Settlement dismissed the application holding that the property in question is an abandoned property. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement the present petitioners moved this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule.

7. Annexure-A is a photo copy of the deed dated 13-2-1943 in between the Sree Sree Gouranga Dev Bigraha (Deity) and Sreemati Hemangini Devi. Annexure-B is the copy of the deed of perpetual lease in favour of late Md. Ishaque which was given by Sree Sree Gouranga Dev Bigraha (Deity). This registered deed is dated 7-4-1958. Annexure-G is the registered sale deed dated 7-4-1958 in favour of late Md. Ishaque. Annexure-D dated 26-3-1972 shows that the petitioner No.1 Akhtari Begum, wife of late Md. Ishaque, filed an application before the Sub-Divisional Officer Sadar (South), Dhaka for releasing her house No. 51, Bonogram Road, PS Sutrapur, Dhaka, from the list of abandoned properties, Annexure-E shows that petitioner No. 1 was asked by the Ministry to submit the papers and documents by a letter dated 15-11-75. Annexure-F is another letter addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development, dated 18-9-1976 by which the petitioner No.1 made a prayer for releasing her property at 51, Bonogram Road, Dhaka. Annexure-G series are the copies of the depositions of two witnesses in favour of the petitioners before the Court of Settlement including the petitioner No.1 Akhtari Begum and the deposition of Md. Khalil who deposed on behalf of the Government. Annexure-H is the judgment of the Court of Settlement. Annexure-I is a deed of dissolution of partnership in between Md. Ishaque and Md. Khalil.

8. It is not disputed that late Md. Ishaque was the original owner of the property in question at 51, Bonogram Road, Dhaka by virtue of lease and he owned and possessed the said property by himself and by leasing out some portion to several tenants. It is also not disputed that late Md. Ishaque lived there with his wife and children. It is also not disputed that after the death of Md. Ishaque in 1967 the heirs of Md. Ishaque namely, the petitioners, lived there and the tenants paid rents to the petitioner No.1 who is the wife of late Md. Ishaque. It is the case of the petitioners that at the time of independence of Bangladesh they had to leave that house in order to save their lives as some miscreants forcibly took possession of the house and petitioner No.1 along with her children took shelter at Mohammadpur in the house of younger brother of late Md. Ishaque. After going there the petitioner No.1 in the month of March, 1972 filed the first application before the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, (South), Dhaka, for releasing the property in her favour stating that she along with her children till date were living and residing in Bangladesh. It appears that the property was taken over as abandoned property and the existing tenants became the tenants of the Government who had been paying rent to the Government being allottees of the Government.

9. The Court of Settlement after hearing the parties and perusing the papers held that the petitioners were the citizens of Pakistan and as they failed to manage and control the property in question, the property was rightly declared and taken over as abandoned property. Mr. MA Wahab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that admittedly the petitioners are the legal heirs of original owner late Md. Ishaque and they never left this country and went to Pakistan and living here they were trying their best to get the property released from the list of abandoned properties.

10. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the respondents. His main contention is that since there are several questions of facts and since those facts have been decided by the Court of Settlement, the same cannot be challenged in writ jurisdiction. Learned Additional Attorney-General submits that whether the petitioners left Bangladesh 2/3 months before the liberation, whether the petitioners were and are present in Bangladesh after liberation, whether the petitioner No.1 put her signature in Urdu or put her LTI, whether petitioner No.1 Akhtari Begum filed applications in 1972, 1975 and 1978 and whether the person was brought to Court was actually lqbal or not, all these are disputed questions of fact and since the same have been decided against the petitioner by the Court of Settlement, this court in Writ Jurisdiction cannot interfere with the judgment of the Court of Settlement inasmuch as this Writ Court is not a Court of appeal over the Court of Settlement. In support of his contention Mr. Bhuiyan has referred to several decisions in the case of Hosna Ara Begum vs. Chairman, Court of Settlement, 46 DLR (AD) 9; Mustafa Kamal vs. 1st Court of Settlement 48 DLR (AD) 61; CQMH Md. Ayub Ali, vs. Bangladesh and others 47 DLR (AD) 71; Ayesha Salahuddin vs. Chairman, 2nd Labour Court, 32 DLR (AD) 68; Farid Miah. vs. Amfad Ali, 42 DLR (AD) 12; New India Tea Company vs. Bangladesh, 31 DLR (AD) 303; and Government of Bangladesh vs. Chand Miah, 44 DLR (AD) 98.

11. It is not established principle that if any Tribunal decided a question of fact, the same cannot be agitated in writ jurisdiction and as regards the question of fact the Tribunal is the final authority and the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that in all the aforesaid decisions it is clearly settled that the disputed question of facts cannot beagitated in writ jurisdiction and on the basis of the above principles this writ petition is not maintainable and the judgment of the Court of Settlement should be upheld.

<u>12. Mr. MA Wahab Miah is not disputing with the above principles settled by our Appellate Division, but he has referred to 15 BLD (AD) 175, particularly, paragraph 16. Paragraph 16 of the aforesaid decision of 15 BLD (AD), 175 runs as follows :</u>

<u>"........The High Court Division was not a Court of Appeal required to make determination of facts on its own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it could be shown that the Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act of without jurisdiction."</u>

<u>13. Relying on the aforesaid decision the learned Advocate submits that the finality of the decision of the Court of Settlement is undoubtly there, but in writ jurisdiction this Court can interfere into the matter if there arises a question of non-consideration of evidence or the question of no evidence or the question of misconstruction of the evidence. Mr M A Wahab Miah has relied upon this principle settled by our Appellate Division and submitted that there are some non-consideration of evidence as well as misconstruction of evidence and as such, the petitioners are entitled to challenge the judgment of the Court of Settlement. Mr. MA Wahab Miah further submits that since both the petitioners arc citizens of Bangladesh and since they never went to Pakistan renouncing the citizenship of this country and accepted the citizenship of Pakistan and since they are still living in Bangladesh, they cannot be treated as Pakistani citizens and their aforesaid property cannot be declared to be an abandoned property, although for the time being they had to leave the property due to circumstances beyond their control. He further submits that since 1972 the petitioners have been submitting representation after representation to the authority stating that they are Bangladeshi nationals living within Bangladesh. But without considering that aspect the authority treated the property of the petitioners as abandoned property. Mr. MA Wahab Miah has also referred to President''s Order 149 of 1972 and submitted that in view of the provisions of this Presidential order the petitioners are the citizens of Bangladesh. He further submits that though for the time being due to unavoidable circumstances beyond control they had to leave the property and went elsewhere and since in the eye of law they are the citizens of Bangladesh, their property cannot be treated as abandoned property under President''s Order 16 of 1972 inasmuch as the property has not acquired in any manner the character of abandoned property.</u>

<u>14. Mr Wahab on the basis of the observation of their Lordships as quoted above, submits that in the instant case there are non-consideration as well as misconstruction of evidence on record which called for interference by this Court. PWs 1 and 2 in this case in unequivocal language stated that the petitioners are the citizens of Bangladesh. Petitioner No.1 Akhtari Begum stated that she lived in section 11, Mirpur, Dhaka, with the brother of her late husband. Her son is Iqbal. She never went to Pakistan. Her son was also present in Court. She cannot read and write and that is why she always put LTI. She never went to Pakistan. In cross-examination she stated about the death of her other children. She admitied the fact that she entered into an agreement with Mesbahuddin for selling some portion of the land. She is an old lady of about 70 years. Mesbahuddin possessed his land which he purchased from her. PW 2, Md. Khalil, is the younger brother of her late husband Md. Ishaque. She corroborated in all material particulars with the PW 1. His statements in all material particulars support the case of the petitioners.</u>

15. DW 1 is one Abdur Rashid Khan. Admittedly he was a tenant in the premises. He stated that before independence of Bangladesh the petitioners went to Pakistan. He admitted that the petitioners are the heirs of late Md. Ishaque and they are the owners of the premises 51, Bonogram Road. About two months before the independence of Bangladesh the petitioners were found in that premises. Thereafter petitioner No. 1 with her children went to Pakistan. About 12/13 years ago he went to Pakistan and he saw the petitioners there in a house. In cross examination he stated that he was brought by one Abdul Gaffar, another tenant of the house, to depose in this case. He stated—" আমি অত্র আদালতে গত তারিখে যে আক্তারী বেগমকে দেখিয়াছি বর্তমান মামলার দরখাস্তকারী সেই আক্তারী বেগম। নালিশী বাড়ীর মালিক আজ আদালত হাজির আছে।”

16. Mr. Wahab submits that he is a hostile tenant and he admitted before the Court that the owner of the house was very much present in the Court. This evidence was totally ignored and non-considered by the Court of Settlement. Another DW named Muslim Ali Khan. He was one of the tenants of that premises. He also admitted that Akhtari Begum is the owner of the premises, but she went to Karachi. But Akhtari Begum was very much present in Court and this Akhtari Begum is the owner of the house. He is one of the allottees of the house in question. He did not know when and how Akhtari Begum left this country. He knew that Akhtari Begum lived in Mirpur. Mr Wahab submits that he is a hostile tenant and present allottee of the premises in question and he admitted Akhtari Begum as the owner and he further admitted that Akhtari Begum lived at Mirpur. So, this portion of the evidence of DW 2 has not been considered by the Court of Settlement. Mr. Wahab submits that since both the DWs who deposed in favour of the Government know Akhtari Begum and admitted that she was present in Bangladesh living at Mirpur and they admitted that she being the owner of the house, filed the application before the Court of Settlement had not been considered by the Court of Settlement and if considered the decision might have been otherwise.

17. It is stated in the judgment that the tenants produced several rent receipts before the Court of Settlement, but no receipts are found in the record. The Court of Settlement found that Akhtari Begum had put her signature in Urdu, but she put LTI in all the relevant papers as well as in the application before the Court of Settlement. So, this Akhtari Begum was not the owner of the premises and she went to Karachi. Merely it is alleged that she put her signature in Urdu and now she put her LTI in the documents, the conclusion cannot be drawn that she left this country and she lived at Karachi as a citizen of Pakistan. The Court failed to exercise its jurisdiction by not examining the LTI of Akhtari Begum with the admitted LTI by any expert. Had there been any doubt about the LTI and identity of Akhtari Begum, then the Court ought to have examined the admitted LTI with the disputed LTI of Akhtari Begum by the expert. But the Court failed to exercise its jurisdiction in that respect also.

18. Now the question arises, on behalf of the Government two persons deposed who are very much interested witnesses in view of the fact that previously they were the hostile tenants of Akhtari Begum and now allottees of the Government. It is the case of Akhtari Begum that at the instigation of the tenants the property was declared as abandoned property, but the fact remains that the tenants admitted her as the owner of the property. Their allegations is that she left for Karachi, but in their depositions they stated that the owner Akhtari had appeared before the Court and she filed the case before the Court of Settlement and she lived at Mirpur. Since the petitioners filed before the Court all the relevant old documents of the premises in question and since the petitioner No. 1 filed an application on 26-3-72, another application on15-11-75 and another application on 18-9-76 for releasing the property from the list of abandoned properties, it appears to us that the two oral evidence, namely, evidence of DWs. 1 and 2, together with the documentary evidence clearly show that the petitioners are still living in Bangladesh as citizens of Bangladesh. The petitioners adduced oral evidence supported by the documentary evidence, but the defendant adduced two oral evidence only who are highly interested person being hostile tenants in the house in question. We will discuss about the malafide intention of the tenants later on.

19. Court of Settlement discussed the oral evidence as well as the documentary evidence adduced before it, but it lost sight of one thing that, if the admitted owner lived in this country and she appeared before the Court of Settlement with her son and produced all the old documents of the house in question before the Court, how the "petitioners would be declared as citizens of Pakistan and their property would be taken over as abandoned property ? In this connection we may refer to President''s Order 149 of 1972 where Article 2 provides that a person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh whose father or grandfather was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March, 1971, and continues to be so resident; or who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971, and continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force. So, from the evidence of the two DWs. it appears that about two months before independence of Bangladesh, this Akhtari Begum left the house. It could not be proved by any evidence to show that how they left this country and went to Karachi. So, it is admitted by the two DWs that Akhtari Begum was the owner of the house and she left the house about two months before independence, that is, before 16th December, 1971. So, it clearly shows that on 25th day of March, 1971, the petitioners were the permanent residents of Bangladesh and they resided in that house, namely, 51, Sonogram Road.

<u>20. Of the two petitioners, petitioner No. 2 was born in the territory of this country and he was permanent resident on 25th day of March, 1971. Now considering the material evidence or record as well as the provisions of Article 2 of President''s Order 149 of 1972 it clearly appears to us that in the eye of law the petitioners are the citizens of Bangladesh and they are living in the territory of Bangladesh and as such, the property of the petitioners, namely, 51 Bonogram Road cannot be taken over as abandoned property in view of the fact that it has not assumed the character of abandoned property. This part of legal position has been totally ignored by the Court of Settlement.</u>

21. As regards managing and occupying the property it appears that at the relevant time, that is, in 1971, it was not possible for the petitioners to live at Bonogram Road and she admitted that out of fear and in order to save their lives they shifted to Mirpur in the house of their relation and from there they have been trying hard even from 1972 to get the property released from the list of abandoned property. In support of that they have filed several copies of applications as well as the letters issued by the Government asking them to produce their documents. But the difficulty was there that the Government issued their letters at the address of 51, Bonogram Road, Dhaka. Unfortunately, the petitioners were living at Mirpur and the hostile tenants of the petitioners suppressed those letters of the Government. Be that as it may, since it appears from material evidence on record that both the petitioners did not leave this country and both of them lived at Mirpur area in their relation''s house since December, 1971 and since they are very much present in Bangladesh and they appeared before the Court of Settlement, filed their application for release of this property and deposed before the Court as witness, we are of the view that the present property has not assumed the character of abandoned property under President''s Order 16 of 1972.

22. Thq Respondent No. 2 in this case has filed the supplementary-affidavit with some documents. From Annexure-I to this supplementary affidavit it shows that eight persons filed a suit being Title Suit No. 374 of 1989 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka. In that suit Md. Iqbal was defendant No. 2 and Musammat Akhtari Begum was the defendant No. 3. Their address was shown at 51, Gour Nitai Shah Road, at present 51, Bonogram Road, PS Sutrapur, Dhaka. The plaintiffs in that suit are the tenants and allottees in the aforesaid premises, namely 51, Bonogram Road. Knowing it fully well that Iqbal and Akhtari Begum were not residing at 51, Banogram Road, the plaintiffs had given their address at 51, Bonogram Road, and they cause the serviced return unserved on the allegation that they left this country and lived in Pakistan. Muslim Ali Khan is plaintiff No. 1 in that suit who was DW 2 in the Court of Settlement. Plaintiff No. 2, Md. Gaffar of that suit brought another allottee in the Court who deposed as DW 1. So, it appears that all the hostile tenants of the petitioners who are living at 51, Bonogram Road, were the plaintiffs and knowing it fully well that the petitioners were living elsewhere the plaintiffs wrote their address at 51, Bonogram Road, with ulterior motive. The prayer made in that suit is very interesting which runs as follows:

“অতএব, বাদীগন প্রার্থনা করেন যে,

(ক) পি,ও, ১৬/৭২ এর আওতায় ও ২৩/৯/৯৬ইং তারিখের বাংলাদেশ গেজেট নোটিফিকেশন এর ভিত্তিতে নালিশী সম্পত্তিটি প্রকৃত মালিক বাংলাদেশ সরকার বলিয়া স্থিরতর ও দৃঢ়তর করার ঘোষণা দিতে মর্জি হয়।

(খ) বাদীগন সরকারের অধিনে বৈধ ভাড়াটিয়া ও দখলকার বলিয়া ঘোষণা ও আদেশ প্রদান করিতে মর্জি হয়।

(গ) দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমা নং ৩৯৬/৮৭ মোকদ্দমার প্রদত্ত ২৫/১/৮৮ ইং তারিখের রায় ও ডিক্রী বাদিদের উপর প্রযোজ্য ও বাধ্য নহে এবং দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমা নং ৩৯৬/৮৭ তে প্রদত্ত ডিক্রীটি বাতিল (set aside)করিবার ঘোষণা ও আদেশ দিতে মর্জি হয়।

23. This suit was decreed ex parte in view of the fact that notices were not served upon the defendants as because the defendants were not there. Decree was passed in accordance with the prayer made in the plaint. In the decree the plaintiff-tenants were declared as the allottees of the Government and it was further declared that the property was an abandoned property. It is very curious to note that all the hostile tenants of the present petitioners filed the above suit for declaration that the property in question should be declared as abandoned property, though it was already declared as abandoned property and they were living there as allottees of the Government and further they prayed for a decree that they should be treated as allottees of the Government and subsequently ex parte decree was passed in that manner.

<u>24. Such a curious and peculiar suit filed by the hostile tenants of the petitioners is unheard of. It clearly shows that the tenants with malafide intention to grab the property filed the aforesaid suit and obtained the ex parte decree. Further, two tenants appeared as witnesses on behalf of the Government in the Court of Settlement. Since they were so highly interested persons and since the suit is a very peculiar one as because the property was previously declared as abandoned property but even then it was prayed for in the suit that the property should be declared as abandoned property and they should be declared as allottees of the Government, it goes to show the malafide character of hostile tenants of the petitioners who were living there at the relevant time at 51, Bonogram Road. So, the Court of Settlement, in fact, acted without jurisdiction in accepting the evidence of the two hostile tenants who always acted malafide in order to grab the property of the present petitioners, Decree passed in the above suit is ex fade redundant. Be that as it may, since we hold that the petitioners are still the citizens of this country, their property can never be declared as abandoned property and,as such, the judgment of the Court of Settlement is liable to be set aside.</u>

25. Mr. Wahab has relied upon the decisions in the cases of Government of Bangladesh vs. M/s Ispahani, 40 DLR (AD) 116, Government of Bangladesh vs. Speed Bird Navigation, 30 DLR (SC) 101; Government of Bangladesh vs. ATJ Industries, 28 DLR (AD) 120 and Bangladesh vs. Professor Golam Azam, 46 DLR (AD) 192. He also relied upon Article 2 of President''s Order 149 of 1972 and submitted that the petitioners cannot be treated as citizens of Pakistan. Rather they are the legal and real citizens of Bangladesh. Relying on the principles settled by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the aforesaid cases and also on the basis of the Article 2 of President''s Order 149 of 1972 we are of the view that the submissions of Mr. Wahab have got substance and the said decisions are applicable in the present case. As such, we hold that the petitioners are citizens of Bangladesh.

26. We have also carefully considered the judgment of the Court of Settlement. We find all the old documents of the property in possession of the petitioners. Findings of LTIs. and signatures in Urdu (as alleged) cannot go to a conclusion that the petitioners are citizens of Pakistan and their property is an abandoned property. Further, the alleged LTI were not sent to the expert for examination. Non-submission of voters'' list and Ration Cards does not also mean to include the property as abandoned property as it is not required under Article 2 of President''s Order 16 of 1972. Findings as regards the citizenship of the petitioners and their education, etc. are absolutely based on presumption without being supported by any material and legal evidence on record.

27. Applications of the petitioners to the SDO and the Government dated 26-3-72, 4-11-75, 18-9-76, 7-12-77, 11-10-86 together with documents and papers viz, Mutation Case No. 1020/88, Certified copy of CS Khatian issued on 27-7-86, certified copy of SA Khatian issued on 27-7-86, Certified copy of ex parte decree and order sheet of TS No. 160/72, Certified copy of Title Execution Case No. 9/75, Mutation of Khatian in the name of the petitioners dated 24-6-76, Rent Receipts for payment of rent, Certified copy of RS Khatian, mutation of the name of the petitioners in the records of Dhaka Municipal Corporation on 7-3-78, Receipts for payment of Municipal taxes, Certified copies of the dismissal order of the application and the order sheet of the Misc. Case filed for setting aside the ex parte decree and the agreement of Akhtari Begum with Mesbahuddin Ahmed dated 29-4-70 clearly show that the petitioners are the citizens of Bangladesh and they all have been residing in Bangladesh althrough and they never left for Pakistan.

28. It is really a curious judgment passed by the Court of Settlement. In the body of the judgment the discussions of the Court of Settlement go to show that it was arriving at a decision that the petitioners are citizens of this country and, as such, their property cannot assume the character of abandoned property as contemplated under Article 2 of President''s Order 16 of 1972. But abruptly it reached conclusion saying that "in view of the above findings I am of the opinion that the petitioners of the case No. 190 of 1987 are Pakistani Nationals : by operation of President''s Order 149 of 1972 and left this country for Pakistan during the War of Liberation of this country, never returned to this country until before hearing of this case." Such findings and conclusion are contrary to the material evidence on record and, as such, the Judgment of the Court of Settlement cannot be sustained. Court of Settlement misinterpreted and misconstrued the provision of President''s Order 149 of 1972, which, in our opinion, are in favour of the petitioners showing that they are the citizens of Bangladesh.

29. In Writ Petition No. 1876 of 1992 the petitioner also challenged the aforesaid judgment of the Court of Settlement. It is his case that Akhtari Begum entered into an agreement in 1970 in order to sell a portion of the spit property and since she failed to execute and register the sale deed, he filed a suit for specific performance of contract and ultimately got a decree and through Court a deed of sale had already been registered in his favour. Akhtari Begum admitted the agreement. In this case one question is very pertinent in view of the fact that agreement was entered into in 1970 and in that agreement Akhtari Begum put her LTI and not the signature in Urdu. The abandoned property law came into force in the year 1972. In the year 1970 while petitioner No. 1 Akhtari Begum wanted to sell a portion of her property, she put her LTI in the deed of agreement. So, it appears that even from the year 1970 Akhtari Begum used to put her LTI on the document which shows that she is illiterate and she never signed the rent receipts in Urdu. It clearly proves that Akhtari Begum used to put her LTI al through in the subsequent documents even in the application before the Court of Settlement. The Vokalatnama submitted before this Court as well as the affidavit sworn by them in the instant Writ Petition and the copy of passport of petitioner No. 2 Iqbal show that they always put their LTIs as they are illiterate. The petitioner of this writ petition will in fact rise and fall with the fate of Akhtari Begum. Since we have already held that the petitioners of other Writ Petition Akhtari Begum and her son are the citizens of Bangladesh and their property cannot be declared as abandoned property, we are of the view that the petitioner in this case will also succeed along with Akhtari Begum and her son.

30. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute and the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement are hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to release the property in favour of the petitioners in both the writ petitions within sixty days from the date of receipt of the Copy of this judgment.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case we pass no order as to cost.

End.
